## Snapshot
Micron is one of three scaled DRAM makers (with Samsung and SK Hynix) and a top-tier NAND supplier, selling DRAM/NAND/NOR under the Micron and Crucial brands (FY25 10-K, 2025-10-03). DRAM is ~79% of revenue, NAND ~20-21% (Q2 FY26, 2026-03-18) — 🆕 **73% / 26% in F4Q26** (Micron FQ4-26 prepared remarks, 2026-09-30). The franchise is reorganized around four data-center-centric BUs: Cloud Memory (CMBU), Core Data Center (CDBU), Mobile & Client (MCBU), and Auto & Embedded (AEBU). The thesis hinges on memory being repositioned "from a system component to a strategic asset" for AI — Micron supplies the full memory hierarchy that agentic inference consumes: HBM next to the accelerator, LPDDR/DDR5/SoCAM expansion memory on the CPU, and high-capacity QLC/TLC data-center SSDs for the growing KV-cache/context tier (Sathya Kumar via UBS Arcuri call, 2026-05-15). It is the #2-3 HBM player behind SK Hynix; only credible third source on HBM4 given Samsung's product issues.

## At a glance — product · buyer · supplier
| | |
|---|---|
| **Sells (top 3)** | 1) DRAM (~79% rev, incl. HBM) · 2) HBM (margin-accretive AI memory, share≈DRAM share) · 3) NAND/eSSD (~20-21% rev) |
| **Main buyer(s)** | Hyperscalers + AI accelerator OEMs (NVIDIA/AMD) for HBM; mobile/client + auto/embedded OEMs; supply-constrained — fills only 50-66% of key-customer demand, CY26 HBM sold out |
| **Key suppliers** | TSMC (HBM4 base die, N12/N3) + IP partners for leading-edge logic; ASML EUV tools (1γ DRAM); cleanroom/fab construction |

**🆕 2026-08-27 — THE RUBIN ULTRA 8-Hi DE-SPEC, QUANTIFIED — READ-THROUGH, NOT A COMPANY DATAPOINT.** ⚠️⚠️ **DAMNANG (Substack) — INDEPENDENT AUTHOR, NOT A BROKER: no rating, no PT, no model; the 8-Hi premise is self-described as *"UNCONFIRMED information based on industry checks"* and the revenue figures as *"scenario SENSITIVITIES, not company guidance or shipment forecasts."*** ("What Does Rubin Ultra's 8-Hi HBM Mean?", 2026-08-10 · "HBM Density Peak", 2026-08-20 — full working is on [[SKHYNIX]] and [[NVDA]]) [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/What_Does_Rubin_Ultras_8-Hi_HBM_Mean__-_Damnangs_Substack.html) · [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/HBM_Density_Peak__Why_AI_Value_Is_Moving_From_Memory_to_Connectivity.html)
- 🔴 **THE HEADLINE FOR ANY HBM SUPPLIER: HBM REVENUE FALLS FAR LESS THAN THE BIT COUNT, AND MAY NOT FALL AT ALL.** 12-Hi → 8-Hi lifts effective output ~**1.63x** (up to 1.5x stacking time × 1.084x stack yield at 98% per-core-die). If [[NVDA]] absorbs it all into extra GPU shipments, **total HBM revenue lands at ~81.5% of plan at 8-Hi pricing of 50% of planned HBM4E, and ~98% at 60%** — versus the naive bits-based ~73%. The naive number is too bearish because *"the CORE DIE COUNT is 8 versus 12, about two thirds, and the BASE DIE goes in the same"* either way. ➤ **The falsifiable bar: *"if 12-Hi HBM4E could not actually meet more than 81.5% of the required volume, this despec can actually result in HIGHER revenue."***
- 🔴 **THE COMPETITIVE AXIS SHIFTS, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR THIS PAGE: *"In the regime where 12-Hi and 16-Hi stack height was itself the AXIS OF DIFFERENTIATION, high-stack qualification and stacking technology carried a LARGE PREMIUM. Directionally favourable to a share challenger, unfavourable to whoever was earning a high-stack premium.** ⚠️ **Directional only. No share forecast, no ASP, no volume, and the underlying spec is unconfirmed — three independent sources this week ([[NVDA]] itself via MS, Jefferies' conference recap, and this author) all say the Rubin Ultra configuration is NOT FINAL.**
- **THE CAUSE IS A QUALIFICATION FAILURE, NOT A DEMAND FAILURE:** NVDA has been asking **~16Gbps pin speed on HBM4E**, and *"the HBM4E samples submitted so far by the THREE MEMORY MAKERS are reportedly having a harder time than expected passing qualification at that spec"*, against HBM4 already holding **10-11Gbps vs an 8Gbps JEDEC baseline**. ⚠️ **The author cautions the newly requested HBM4 pin speed *"comes close to the 15 to 16Gbps"* asked of 4E — so the HBM4 / HBM4E label is NOT a clean bandwidth distinction and must not be used as one in a bit or ASP model.** ✅ **Independently corroborated in direction by Jefferies (08-27): the de-spec is *"a means of STRETCHING A CONSTRAINED DIE POOL and INCREASING ACCELERATOR SHIPMENTS… it does not undermine structural bit growth and, if anything, REINFORCES that demand is running ahead of available supply."***

**🆕🔴 2026-08-23 — HOT CHIPS: MICRON PUT HARD NUMBERS ON WHY HBM IS EATING THE DRAM INDUSTRY'S WAFERS, AND THE RATIO IS GETTING WORSE, NOT BETTER.** (Speaker: Ragu, Micron HBM Design Architecture, via TMT Breakout "Hot Chips Takeaways", 2026-08-23; viksnewsletter, 2026-08-24; jasonschips "Hot Chips Day 1 — Precious Memories", 2026-08-24 — **conference-coverage newsletters, NOT broker research.**)
- 🔴 **"MU has previously quantified HBM3E at roughly 3x the silicon of DDR5 for the same bits. Ragu said that ratio is not improving and is likely getting worse as bandwidth increases."** More parallelism → larger dies, more supporting circuitry, and taller stacks add yield challenges.
- 🔴 **"Memory can represent roughly 90% of the silicon in a high-end AI package":** in a representative GPU package with **four 12-high HBM stacks, total memory silicon can be roughly 8x the GPU silicon.** Reliability consequence stated bluntly: **one failing DRAM die can affect the entire package.**
- **Reliability is already showing up in production:** Ragu cited **META's published Llama 3 work, where roughly 17% of unintended training interruptions were attributed to HBM.** HBM3/3E added metadata for CRC and system-level ECC alongside on-die symbol-based ECC and Reed-Solomon protection; MU expects RAS mechanisms to keep advancing.
- **Stack-height ceiling, stated by the vendor:** **16-high looks achievable; beyond that is "less clear"** — die thinning, mechanical stress and thermal resistance get much harder. **JEDEC has discussed 20-high, but "substantial work remains after 16."** The binding constraints are **TSV density, power density, thermals, mechanical integrity and yield** — *not* signalling distance (the whole stack stays under ~1mm).
- **The bandwidth arithmetic:** **HBM3E 128 banks per DRAM die → HBM4 256**; external interface **~1,000 → ~2,000 I/O lines within roughly the same shoreline**; cumulative scaling from **HBM1 at 128 GB/s and 1GB to HBM4 at >2.8 TB/s and >24GB per cube** — "at the cost of much higher silicon intensity."
- **Thermals are now first-order:** the base die is the hottest area (highest-speed D2D links plus increasingly complex logic), heat is generated at the bottom while cooling sits above the stack, so **each additional DRAM die adds thermal resistance.** MU says HBM is now **architected around thermal limits from the start.**
- **Two forward-looking claims worth tracking:** HBM may become **more workload-specific** (different bank structures, channel counts, access granularities per AI workload, with processor and memory co-optimised); and packaging is **shifting from micro-bumps and thermal-compression bonding toward fusion and hybrid bonding at single-digit-micron pitches.** Filed also to themes/hbm-memory and themes/cowos-packaging.
- **The independent framing that ties it together (Jim Handy, Objective Analysis, same conference):** **HBM produces roughly one-third as many gigabytes per wafer as standard DDR**; DRAM suppliers went **more than a decade without major capacity additions** because shrinks sufficed; **new fabs take ~2 years even on aggressive timelines**, leaving the industry unable to respond to a demand shock. He also makes the anti-Jevons argument explicitly: *"If an algorithm improves efficiency by 6x, the result may be 6x more output rather than lower capex."*

**🆕⚠️ 2026-07-27 (SWEPT ~25 DAYS LATE) — THE CXMT-LISTING BEAR CASE ARRIVES ON THE PAGE, AND THE AUTHOR TESTS EVERY LEG OF IT AND REJECTS EVERY LEG. THE PRICE MARKS BELOW ARE HISTORICAL; THE FRAMEWORK IS THE VALUE.** (DAMNANG — an INDEPENDENT SUBSTACK AUTHOR (damnang2.substack.com), "After CXMT's Listing, Do the Memory Three Have Further to Fall?", 2026-07-27. **NOT a broker: no rating, no PT, no model; the author discloses he "may hold positions in the companies mentioned."**)
- **The event, which this page has carried only as a Catalysts line, now with the tape attached: "In mid-July 2026, when CXMT confirmed its listing date, Micron fell 8% and lost one trillion dollar[s of] market capitalization, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix [sold] off alongside it. The threat of Chinese memory had landed as a psychological shock." Then "on 27 July CXMT opened at 49.50 yuan, 472% above its IPO price of 8.66," an RMB3.31tn (~US$489bn) market cap that "made it the most valuable company listed on the A-share market," reaching RMB54.65 (+531%) by midday with "more than 1[xx] billion yuan traded in half a session" and foreign investors net sellers of Samsung and SK hynix the same day.**
- 🔴 **THE VERDICT IS THE POINT, AND IT IS A REBUTTAL — DO NOT READ THIS NOTE AS AN ENDORSEMENT OF THE BEAR CASE. The author states the market's worry in one sentence ("that CXMT will break DRAM prices and shrink the profits of Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron"), lists the claims that support it, and then knocks each one down:**
  - **① "CXMT sells 30% below the incumbents" — a COMPANY-AVERAGE artifact. "It compares CXMT's company-wide average selling price against the company-wide average selling price of the three incumbents. The gap is that wide because roughly two thirds of CXMT's revenue comes from low-priced mobile memory." Like-for-like "the gap is 5% to 10% per the prospectus CXMT filed for its listing, and in server products the sign flips altogether": in July 2026 a 64GB DDR5 server module built with CXMT chips sold for RMB18,999 in Chinese online retail versus RMB18,595 on Samsung/SK hynix chips — **CXMT 2.2% HIGHER** — and in the contract market "CXMT was reported to have quoted above Samsung's supply price of 1,240 dollars per module."**
  - **② It CANNOT cut price, because of cost: "At its current level of technology, CXMT spends more than 30% more than the incumbents to produce the same amount of memory. Its chips are about 40% larger in area, and its yield… falls short of the 85% to 90% the industry treats as standard."**
  - **③ "It already holds 8% of the market" — that is a REVENUE number and revenue inflates with price. CXMT booked $7.31bn of DRAM revenue in Q1-2026 = 7.7% of the world market; but on OUTPUT it "puts 13% of the world's DRAM wafers into production and turns them into 6% of the memory capacity… half of what goes in disappears on the way from wafers to capacity." And its startling Q1-2026 revenue growth (+71[x]% y/y) was price, not volume: measured q/q, "the memory capacity it shipped grew only 11% while its average selling price rose 57%."**
  - **④ "IPO proceeds will flood the market with supply" — wrong clock. "Turning IPO proceeds into equipment orders and equipment into production takes 18 to 24 months, so… the supply this listing funds arrives in 2028 at the earliest." On the reported (Goldman-sourced, which he explicitly says he "cannot verify") "double DRAM capacity by 2030" story: "what doubles is the number of wafers, not the memory capacity… Doubling the wafers still leaves it near 12% on a capacity basis, and over those four years DRAM demand is set to grow far faster than that." He reads it as good news for Chinese equipment makers (Naura, AMEC) rather than bad news for the memory three — and takes a swipe at the transmission mechanism: pieces "written by press outlets and institutions without the technical background to write them, vague and rounded off, circulating as though [they] were established fact… the distortion reaches share prices."**
  - **⑤ "It is catching up in HBM" — not on this evidence: CXMT "allocates less than 2% of its total wafer starts to HBM," "its HBM3 schedule slipped on thermal problems," and combined yield on the eight-high product is "estimated at around 25%" against 70-90% at the incumbents. And the SIGN OF THE EFFECT INVERTS: "As CXMT shifts more capacity into HBM, ordinary DRAM prices come under UPWARD pressure rather than downward," because stacking consumes ~3x the wafer area per GB — converting DRAM lines to HBM cuts the ordinary-DRAM capacity off those lines "to one third of what it was."**
  - **On the technology gap, which is the one place he concedes ground and then bounds it: CXMT brought 16nm-class DDR5 to volume on DUV multi-patterning with no EUV option, and the gap "has closed quickly since 2019" — but "CXMT took 18 to 24 months to move from its third process generation to its fourth, and its fifth generation has already run past 24 months," while the incumbents also turn a generation roughly every 24 months. "The fair conclusion is that the three generation gap [to] major memory makers stays where it is," and the RATE of closing "has flattened."**
- 🔴 **THE ONE NUMBER TO LIFT OUT, BECAUSE IT IS THE CLEANEST STATEMENT OF THE CROWDING-OUT MECHANISM THIS PAGE ALREADY RUNS: "In 2026 HBM consumes 22% of global DRAM wafer capacity while producing only 9% of the memory capacity. That gap is the underlying reason ordinary DRAM is short today."** ➤ **Same mechanism as the ODM-sourced crowding-out account logged on 08-20 ("similar to HBM versus D4… no one is going to do general server") — two independent sources, one from the DRAM-capacity side and one from the server-BOM side, arriving at the same explanation for conventional-DRAM ASP strength.**
- **THE MU-SPECIFIC CONCLUSION, AND IT MAKES MU THE LEAST EXPOSED OF THE THREE: "Micron has the least left to lose in China. Its mainland China revenue fell [to] the 7% range after the 2023 purchase ban, and it exited the Chinese server memory business in October 2025… the data center exposure is already gone. It competes with CXMT [for] the same customers outside China, but if the United States moves to exclude Chinese memory from data centers and government procurement, that competition never arrives in North America."** ⚠️ **The pre-ban China-revenue figure is TRUNCATED in the extracted text and is therefore not quoted here.** ⚠️ **The offset, in the author's own framing: "Its multiple, at 6.42 times, is the highest of the three" — versus Samsung at 4.32x and SK hynix at 4.69x on 27 July. Least China risk, least valuation cushion.** For contrast: **SK hynix is "the most insulated" because its earnings are concentrated in HBM, which "CXMT cannot enter" — what moves SK hynix "is [customer capex], not CXMT"; Samsung "is hit first and hardest" because it sells the largest share of its output to Chinese smartphone and PC makers, exactly where CXMT's commodity mobile/PC DRAM competes.**
- **The directional call, recorded for the outcome loop: "My own view is that the recent memory correction is more likely to END after the CXMT [listing] than to continue… for the decline to keep going you need either memory earnings to turn down or AI demand to reverse outright. Neither price nor volume shows any sign of coming down." On CXMT's own stock he expects the first day to mark the high (SMIC's July-2020 debut as the precedent — opened +246%, "never traded above that price again"), with a possible correction "around the first lockup release in January 2027," but no break of the IPO price.** ⚠️⚠️ **STALENESS, FLAGGED: this is a 2026-07-27 view written on the 2026-07-27 tape. It is ~25 days old at ingest, every price mark and multiple in it is HISTORICAL, and it is NOT scored in the Signal-vs-management table as a current signal. It is carried because it is the most complete rebuttal of the CXMT bear case on this page.** [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/13_After_CXMTs_Listing_Do_the_Memory_Three_Have_Further_to_Fall_.html)

**🆕🔴 2026-08-18 (/run-inbox) — THE ROADSHOW THIS PAGE FLAGGED AS A CATALYST HAS REPORTED BACK, AND IT DELIVERS THE THREE THINGS THAT WERE STILL MISSING: WHAT FRACTION OF THE SCAs IS *UNPRICED*, WHY RPO UNDERSTATES VISIBILITY, AND THE FAB-BY-FAB CAPACITY LADDER. THE PT IS UNCHANGED — AND THE VALUATION METHOD REVEALS UBS IS NOT CAPITALISING PEAK EARNINGS AT ALL.** (UBS · **Timothy Arcuri** w/ Gianmarco Vella, Aaryan Wadhwa — "On The Road With Mgmt; Climbing The 'Wall of Worry'", **Buy, PT $1,625 unchanged**, px $1,011.75, 2026-08-17.)
- ✅ **CATALYST CLOSED: this is the readout from the UBS-arranged CFO/IR marketing logged below as a dated catalyst (08-15). All four flagged agenda items — LTAs, pricing, capital allocation, cycle durability — were addressed.**
- ✅🔴 **CORROBORATION FIRST, THEN THE NET-NEW PIECE. UBS reports the SCA split as ~10 points of revenue take-or-pay with NO fixed or pre-contracted pricing, and "of the remaining 40%, an undisclosed portion will carry fixed pricing while another portion will be sold with BANDS (ceiling + floor pricing)."** ➤ **The 40/10/50 split itself is NOT new — Micron IR gave this page the same three tranches on 07-27 (~40% priced-framework + ~10% volume-only take-or-pay + ~50% market). What is new is the composition of the 40: the priced-framework tranche is itself divided between FIXED-price and BANDED contracts, which no source had separated before.** ⚠️ **That distinction matters more than it looks. The 08-15 management disclosure directly below established that SCAs carry a ceiling as well as a floor, and this page has been applying that ceiling to the whole priced tranche. If part of the 40 is fixed-price rather than banded, then within the priced book there is a slice with NO upside participation at all and a slice that participates up to a cap — and only the ~10 take-or-pay points plus the ~50% market book run fully with spot. UBS does not size the fixed-vs-banded split, and management has not. That is now the single largest unquantified input in the SCA structure, ahead of the floor GM level.**
- 🔴 **NET-NEW #2 — RPO IS A FLOOR, NOT A MEASURE, AND MANAGEMENT SAID WHY: the RPO disclosure EXCLUDES the ~10% of revenue sold take-or-pay, and ALSO excludes expected customer allocations beyond ~12 months.** UBS concludes **"MU's future RPO disclosures will capture only a part of the company's actual revenue visibility."** Beyond that, MU has **long-term visibility on bits sold OUTSIDE the SCAs** via agreements carrying no pricing component — *"similar to the LTAs it put in place during COVID."* ➤ **Consequence for anyone comparing memory names on booked backlog: MU's RPO is not comparable to [[AVGO]]'s RPO or to a peer's LTA book, and a low print is not a demand signal. Any RPO-based cross-name screen on this wiki is measuring disclosure policy, not visibility.**
- 🔴 **NET-NEW #3 — THE VALUATION METHOD, AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT A $1,625 PT LOOKS LIKE FROM OUTSIDE: UBS applies ~11× NTM P/E — "in line with MU's three-year historical average" — to a C2029 EPS estimate of ~$165, discounted back to C2028E at a ~12% cost of equity for an implied C2028E EPS value of ~$148.** They anchor on C2029 explicitly because **"by that point, our model assumes a MODERATE MEMORY DOWNCYCLE, albeit with LTAs buoying the company's earnings base."** ➤ **The Street-high-looking PT is built on a POST-DOWNCYCLE year at an average multiple — not on peak earnings at a re-rated multiple. That is a materially more defensible bridge than the headline suggests, and it reframes the bear rebuttal: to break the PT you must break the ~$165 C2029 trough-ish EPS, not argue that FY27/FY28 peak earnings deserve less than 11×.** Consistent with the model's own shape: **UBS revenue goes $285.1bn FY27E → $378.9bn FY28E → $272.5bn FY29E → $250.6bn FY30E — the bull case has the downcycle IN it.**
- ⚠️ **THE BEAR MECHANISM, STATED BY THE BULL, AND IT IS THE NEAR-TERM RISK TO CARRY: "shorter-term investors will remain turned off by PEAKING GROSS MARGINS as more volume moves inside of SCAs struck at pricing from 1-2 QUARTERS AGO."** ➤ **The same instrument that guarantees the floor drags the peak: as SCA mix rises, realised price converges to a lagged strike while spot keeps rising. Margin can roll over while demand is still accelerating — and that is a print-level risk into a quarter where the demand headlines will be excellent.** UBS reads positioning as **"skew[ing] quite cautious"** and calls MU a near-term **"battleground."**
- **The demand/pricing update, which CONFIRMS rather than extends what this page holds:** management now characterises **C2027 supply/demand as EVEN TIGHTER than C2026** (an escalation from the 08-10 fireside language); **still fulfilling LESS THAN 50% of the volumes requested by DC customers** — the third independent restatement of the "half the demand" line now on this page; **HBM gross margins to be driven higher** because existing HBM contracts were signed long ago and their pricing lagged the DDR increases, consistent with **UBSe C2027 industry blended HBM ASP +79% y/y** already carried; and **FY27 capex reiterated at mid-$40bn.**
- 🆕 **THE CAPACITY LADDER, FAB BY FAB — net-new to this page and the cleanest answer yet to "when does supply actually arrive": C2027 brings ID1 (~80k wpm) and Tongluo BROWNFIELD (~40k wpm) online in MID-C2027, plus the start of the Singapore HBM back-end packaging ramp. The meaningful net additions come in C2028 — Tongluo GREENFIELD (~40k wpm, mostly housing EUV) and ID2 (~80k wpm) by C2Q28, with the Hiroshima Fab 15 expansion also landing sometime in C2028.** ➤ **The vast majority of the ramp is weighted to C2028, which is the same year Bernstein's Asia team (07-20, below) says China could become a swing factor and the year UBS's own model turns down. Three independent routes to the same date — C2028 is where this cycle gets decided, and 2027 supply is effectively already set.**
- **Capital allocation — no new buyback, and a deliberate expectation-check: MU reiterated that investment in the business (primarily geographic diversification) remains the top priority "over the next several years," is still not indicating a targeted cash level, and used "gradually" / "over time" language on returning 100% of excess cash.** UBS projects **~$75bn of cash by the end of FQ1:27 (Nov), ahead of the 12/9 expiration of the CHIPS Act share-repurchase limits**, and believes MU will ultimately buy back a very large amount of stock — while explicitly warning investors to **keep expectations in check on the TIMING of any announcement.** ➤ **Dated and checkable: the constraint lifts 2026-12-09. That is the first hard date on the buyback debate this page has carried.** [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/20260818_UBS_MU_Micron_Technology_Inc_-On_The_Road_With_Mgmt-_Climbing_T.html)

- 🔴 **NET-NEW AND QUANTIFIED — THE HBM CANNIBALISATION RATIO, WHICH IS THE SUPPLY MECHANISM BEHIND THE WHOLE DRAM SHORTAGE, AND IT WORSENS BY GENERATION:** *"if we produce **100 bits of HBM, we have to reduce 300 bits of DDR supply** because there is that **3:1 trade ratio between HBM 3E and DDR**. You go to **HBM4 and HBM4E**, by the time you get to 4E, that trade ratio has **worsened to closer to 4:1**. So all of this growth in HBM pressures the supply that is left for everything else, which means that the **wafer supply has to increase dramatically**."* ➜ **This is the single most useful number for sizing the DRAM squeeze: every incremental HBM bit destroys 3-4 conventional DRAM bits. It means HBM4E's ramp is mechanically MORE deflationary to available DDR supply than HBM3E's was, and it explains why conventional DRAM tightness persists even as wafer starts rise. Reads across to [SKHYNIX.md](SKHYNIX.md), [SAMSUNG.md](SAMSUNG.md) and [themes/hbm-memory.md](themes/hbm-memory.md).**

MU) to license it**; however, the emergence of another potential at-scale memory supplier — *if successful* — could ultimately **pressure incumbents** and prompt Korean players to invest in US front-end memory (more likely DRAM). **Memory-market read-throughs (2026-07-06):** SK Hynix expected to **list ADRs (ticker SKHY) on Nasdaq Friday (~Jul 10)** — a memory-cycle positive that would make MU no longer the only US-listed big-3 memory maker; and **Samsung reported preliminary Q2 ahead of consensus** (sales KRW 171T vs KRW 169.2T, OI KRW 89.4T vs KRW 84.2T, via Vital Knowledge) — both reinforce the DRAM up-cycle underpinning MU's thesis (2026-07-06).

The correction's proximate trigger was the **SK Hynix 2Q26 print landing ~8% below consensus** (OP ~W60.4tn, +61% QoQ / +556% YoY vs ~W65tn cons) — but local brokerages (KIS, Mirae) attribute the miss to SKHY's *higher HBM sales mix* (slower HBM ASP hikes vs commodity DRAM), a lower commodity-DRAM price hike vs prior Street, and — notably — the **LTA effect (more stable ASP) starting to kick in**, i.e. a smoothing artifact rather than demand weakness (@jukan05 citing KIS/Mirae, 2026-07-13/14). A read-through supportive of MU's own SCA-driven ASP-smoothing thesis rather than a cycle-turn signal. Separately, **Semiecosystem "Micron Provides Boost For U.S. Silicon Wafer Industry" (2026-07-13)** is a US-wafer-industry read-through corroborating the GlobalWafers/US-ecosystem investment logged above.

**Micron IR call — the most complete SCA disclosure yet, and management walks the tightness horizon forward a third time (Micron IR call · Satish, 2026-07-27).** The second IR call Micron has hosted for a Brazilian institutional-investor audience. Several items sharpen numbers already on this page rather than adding new ones — noted where so:
- **Guidance restated:** Aug-quarter **86% gross margin**, "an increase from the quarter we reported before, which was approximately 85%." On capital: Micron expects "that we will be able to **return 100% of our excess cash to shareholders**" over time.
- **The tightness horizon keeps extending.** Management's own framing has moved **2026 → 2027 (post-earnings) → "beyond calendar 27 and even in 28."** The starkest formulation: "based on our visibility, **we actually do not see a line of sight to when the supply demand balance even comes back into balance**." The *walk-forward itself* is the signal — the level has been revised out at every one of the last three touchpoints. Asked what could normalize the market earlier, Satish pointed to the structural supply governors already on this page (greenfield build time, new nodes not producing as much bit growth, HBM consuming capacity) and to demand "far in excess of supply."
- **SCA architecture, quantified end-state — and it reconciles two figures this page carried side by side.** As of earnings, **25% of revenue committed across 16 contracts, 14 of which carry a pricing framework.** When all planned SCAs are done: **up to 50%+ of total company revenue under SCAs**, split **~40% with a pricing framework (price band or fixed price) + ~10% volume-only take-or-pay with pricing negotiated quarterly (as today)**, leaving **~50% market-priced**. "Probably today that number is in the low 20%" for the framework tranche. _This resolves the page's apparent conflict between management's ">50% of revenue under SCAs" target and Barron's "~40% of revenue once fully executed" — they are the same plan measured on different tranches, not two estimates._ **All SCAs carry take-or-pay volume commitments** — "volume is the key thing that we need to plan our supply."
- **The RPO caveat — it is a floor, not a forecast, and management said so unprompted.** The **~$100bn RPO** across the 14 priced contracts is computed as **contract volume × the FLOOR price**. Satish: "the pricing is at the **ceiling** right now… the revenue that we will actually get on the SCAs, we expect will be **well above the RPO levels**. The RPO is not indicative of the revenue that we will get." Band mechanics: **ceiling ≈ the market price in the June calendar quarter** — "roughly consistent with the type of pricing that we were getting in our results and guidance," i.e. the ceiling is embedded in the 86% GM guide; **floor GM "well above any quarterly cyclical peak gross margin"**, where the prior peak cited is **fiscal 2018, "in the low 60% range"** — "we haven't quantified that level, but we have said it's well above." The band applies for the **entire contract duration** (five years if a five-year deal) on the current product portfolio; a minority of SCAs are fixed-price throughout. On the residual ~50% at market pricing, Micron confirmed it embeds its own price view to get to the "up to 50% or more" claim but "we don't provide a forecast of the revenue of the pricing."
- **China exposure has roughly halved:** from the **high-20s%** two years ago to the **low-double-digit %** today. Two drivers, both named: **Chinese-government restrictions on some Chinese data-center companies buying Micron products**, and Micron's own decision **not to participate in the NAND-flash portion of the mobile market**. Remaining China customers are in **automotive and robotics**.
- **The technology-leadership defence against CXMT/YMTC, given on CXMT's Shanghai debut day.** Micron is **~3 technology nodes ahead** of the Chinese competitors; **1-gamma DRAM (EUV-based) will be more than half of DRAM production around this time of year**, with more EUV use at the next node, **1-delta** — "technologies that are not available outside of in China." Plus **~65,000 patents accumulated over nearly 50 years** and "a historical track record of aggressively defending our patents when we need to." Historical rebuttal offered: two years ago the identical China-supply fear (LPDDR4 into smartphones) was followed by "a historic gap between demand and supply, even with additional capacity that has come from China-based companies."
- **On memory-as-a-commodity:** "the world is actually not black or white… we are increasingly seeing portions of our portfolio where our products are already behaving in a different way" — HBM has had annual volume-and-price contracts for three years with no spot/quarterly market, automotive likewise, and the SCAs now broaden that structure across customers. On double-ordering, Micron says it triangulates customer forecasts against its own market estimate (project tracking, memory intensity per gigawatt, third-party forecasts) rather than taking forecasts at face value. (Micron IR call · Satish, 2026-07-27) [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_27_mu_ir_call_27_jul_26.html)

## HBM technology / share (deep dive)
- **MU's HBM positioning:** Micron leapfrogged in HBM — it skipped standard HBM3 entirely — on the back of a focus on TSVs and the power-delivery network, underpinning its claimed ~30% lower power consumption (claim **explicitly unverified** — SemiAnalysis flags this as an unverified claim, not confirmed) (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.7-8). Micron and Samsung use Non-Conductive Film (NCF) / thermal-compression bonding (TCB) vs Hynix's proprietary MR-MUF molded underfill (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.6). For MU and SK, yield loss on HBM is more than offset by pricing → HBM is margin-accretive; Samsung's worse yields ironically tighten total supply (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.8).
- **HBM4 node choice:** Micron is staying on the **1b node for HBM4** — the same node as SK Hynix — rather than jumping to a new node the way Samsung is attempting with 1c (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.47). Micron **lacks internal advanced-logic design capability** and needs silicon partners/TSMC for the HBM4 custom base die (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.26) — consistent with the base-die logic-gap point below.
- **AMD supply-share shift:** AMD has shifted a significant share of its HBM3E supply **to Micron and away from Samsung** (SemiAnalysis "Scaling the Memory Wall," 2025-08-11, p.46) — a customer-level share data point supporting MU's #2-3 HBM positioning independent of the TAM/pricing commentary elsewhere on this page.
- **HBM4 base die — the key watch item:** the HBM4 base die moves to a modern logic process (TSMC N12 and N3 variants). Pure-memory makers Hynix and Micron lack leading-edge logic design capability and will lean on TSMC + IP partners; only Samsung can build the advanced base die in-house. Custom base dies arrive with HBM4 for NVIDIA/AMD, broadening to other accelerators at HBM4E (~2027); they strengthen vendor lock-in because each is tied to a vendor's proprietary TSV layout (SemiAnalysis, 2025-08-12). Caution flag: Jefferies expert (Inspectrum, 2025-12-17) says **Micron is redesigning its HBM4 base die** to reach speed parity — the two Korean players (esp. Samsung) carry higher confidence on higher speeds, i.e. MU has work to do on the new base die.
- **HBM4 pin-speed execution risk — SemiAnalysis skepticism (net-new, sharper than the Jefferies caution above):** MU's HBM4 samples showed **"much lower pin speeds"** than Samsung/SK Hynix (~10 Gbps); SemiAnalysis is explicitly **"skeptical of execution"** despite management's public confidence, and forecasts **~0% Micron share of Rubin HBM supply in the first 12 months** (SemiAnalysis "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06, p.29). This is a materially more cautious read than the "redesigning for speed parity" framing already on this page and should be weighed as the more bearish end of the HBM4-execution range.
- **★ THE FIRST SUPPLY-CHAIN CHECK ON WHETHER THE PIN-SPEED SKEPTICISM ABOVE WAS RIGHT — and it lands between the two poles (Fubon · Sherman Shang / Arthur (hosted by Jefferies), "industry highlights & checks update", 2026-08-03).** **Verbatim: "from the Rubin HBM side, in the supply chain, we currently only see a SMALL VOLUME OF MICRON AND SAMSUNG'S HBM. And the Rubin with Hynix HBM4 will start to ramp up at LATE AUGUST OR SEPTEMBER WITH A BIGGER VOLUME."** ⚠️ **Read it as a qualification-and-volume statement, not a share statement: MU is *in* — which is better than SemiAnalysis's ~0%-of-first-12-months forecast on the line above — but it is not the vendor pacing the ramp, and Fubon explicitly ties Rubin's back-half weighting (200-300K units in Q3 → 700-800K in Q4) to SK Hynix HBM4 arriving. The honest framing for the model: MU has the design win and is shipping, the volume curve belongs to [[SKHYNIX]], and the gap is the thing to track through Sep-Oct.** **Same call, the execution flag that partly sits inside the HBM stack rather than at NVDA: the ~two-month Rubin production push-out is attributed to "the thermal design change AND THE HBM BASE DIE ISSUE" — the base die being the element MU sources from TSMC (N12/N3) rather than building in-house, per the base-die bullet above.** [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_08_03_sherman_update_03_08_26.html)
- **Fab-timeline detail (SemiAnalysis "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06):** the **A3 fab (Idaho)** is predominantly HBM-allocated; its ramp has been pulled in from 2H27 to **mid-2027**, with wafer output more likely **3Q27** (p.23, 30). The newly acquired **P5 Tongluo fab** (acquired from PSMC) is unlikely to show meaningful output until **2H27**; max capacity ~**45k wafers/month** for commodity DRAM at full utilization, potentially lower if configured for HBM (p.23, 30). SemiAnalysis expects **~30% of DRAM production on the 1c/1γ node by end-2026** (p.24), and pegs **2026 DRAM WFE capex growth at +20%** — the lowest of the three memory makers' capex growth rates (p.34).
- **The HBM4 pin-speed bake-off — the single most useful supplier-side datapoint of the AMD Advancing AI cycle (SemiAnalysis "Can AMD break the CUDA Moat? AMD Advancing AI 2026", 2026-07-24).** AMD's MI455X ships **12 stacks of HBM4 = 432GB per package** and **23.3 TB/s** of memory bandwidth vs **8 stacks / 288GB** on Nvidia Rubin and Google, with Rubin at **22 TB/s** — a near-tie on bandwidth *despite AMD running a 50% wider bus*, because AMD clocks its HBM4 at a pin speed of **7.6 Gbps while Nvidia targets 10.7 Gbps (40% faster)**. SemiAnalysis is explicit that this was a deliberate, supplier-facing decision: "**Nvidia aggressively raised its targeted HBM4 pin speeds last year, well above the original JEDEC HBM4 specification. This change was precisely driven by the need to make up for the memory bandwidth deficit to AMD MI455X.**" The consequence lands directly on the memory makers: the change "**was challenging for memory suppliers to keep up with. Memory suppliers had to rework their HBM4 to deliver the spec Nvidia was targeting. This also pushed out upstream output for Rubin but as of today these issues have been finally resolved**" — and the standing implication is that **Nvidia must use a much higher-quality bin than AMD** for the same HBM4 generation. AMD and Nvidia are the only two shipping HBM4 this year. **Read-through for Micron:** an above-JEDEC pin-speed target means tighter binning, lower effective yield on the top bin, and a widening quality/price spread between suppliers that can hit 10.7 Gbps and those that cannot — a **share-and-mix question, not a volume question**, and the axis on which this page's standing HBM4 pin-speed skepticism (SemiAnalysis "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06: MU samples at "much lower pin speeds," ~0% modeled Rubin share yr-1) is most likely to be resolved either way. _SemiAnalysis does not say which supplier wins the top bin — do not read one in._ Note it also implies a **two-tier HBM4 market by construction**: the AMD 7.6 Gbps socket is a materially easier bin than the Nvidia 10.7 Gbps socket, so a supplier short of Nvidia's spec is not shut out of HBM4 — it is shut out of the *premium* bin. (SemiAnalysis "Can AMD break the CUDA Moat? AMD Advancing AI 2026", 2026-07-24) [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_24_ENC_Can_AMD_break_the_CUDA_Moat_AMD_Advancing_AI_2026_email.html)
  - _Dual-source corroboration:_ the same note's Microsoft/MI300X history (Microsoft dropped AMD after MI300X over "unreliable Samsung 2023 HBM memory") corroborates — rather than adds to — the AMD-shifted-HBM3E-share-to-Micron datapoint already on this page from "Scaling the Memory Wall" (2025-08-11); the current AMD dual-source setup stands, no new share number.
  - _Verification-complexity read-through (one line, different source):_ Micron is named among the memory companies using specialised DRAM/NAND/HBM design tools, where **HBM verification now approaches logic-chip complexity as stacking and interposer-routing requirements grow** — a cost/cycle-time input consistent with the base-die/logic-gap point above (SemiAnalysis "EDA Market Primer", 2026-05-21). [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_05_21_ENC_EDA_Market_Primer_email.html)
- **HBM share (UBS estimates, 2026 overview):** MU HBM bit shipment 0.9 / 4.6 / 7.4 bn Gb (2024/25/26E); HBM as % of MU total DRAM bits 1.5% / 6.2% / 8.4%; MU HBM bit-share of the market ~21-22% in 2026E (vs SK Hynix the leader). MU HBM front-end capacity 30 / 65 / 100 k-wpm (4Q, '24/'25/'26E). Samsung's 2025 HBM share ~20%, "will go up next year" (Jefferies/Inspectrum, 2025-12-17). UBS: MU's HBM business alone supports **$5 / $7+ of EPS in 2026/2027** (~17-18% of EPS), justifying a higher multiple on the segment.

- **Agentic-AI memory-hierarchy sizing (UBS teach-in with MU mgmt, 2026-06-08):** a single agentic prompt can spawn ~4-5 simultaneous agents (each a separate CPU task interfacing with GPU/ASIC), and **query context grows ~30x/yr** — a multiplicative step-up in DRAM capacity, HBM bandwidth, and SSD storage per query. MU quantified the tiers: **HBM-resident active KV cache ~10-100GB/GPU at ~1-20TB/s** (residency ms-to-s); next tier **~200-400GB KV cache/GPU on DRAM at ~100-500GB/s** (s-to-min); **NAND "context memory" tens-to-hundreds of TB** (warm data / vector DB). Products: 192GB SOCAMM already shipping in volume + newly announced 256GB SOCAMM and 256GB RDIMM (**~3x DRAM capacity per CPU socket** vs prior gen); 245TB SSD (rack-level → multi-petabyte AI storage). MU's stance on efficiency (TurboQuant, sparse attention, quantization): gains get reinvested into larger context windows / more agents rather than cutting hardware content (UBS "FQ3:26 preview / agentic teach-in", 2026-06-08). UBS's $1,625 PT = **~15x NTM P/E on C2029E EPS ~$124-125, discounted back** (C2029 is UBS's through-cycle anchor, assuming a moderate downcycle buoyed by LTAs).

- **HBM4/HBM4E primer — MU's place in the 3-supplier universe (Atlas Peak Research "HBM4 and HBM4E: The Memory Wall Becomes the System Architecture Problem," 2026-04-03):** JEDEC finalized HBM4 in April 2025 (2048-bit interface / 32 channels / 2.048 TB/s per stack at the 8 Gb/s baseline — ~2x HBM3E's 1024-bit/1.229 TB/s); HBM4E extends to 16 Gb/s / ~4.096 TB/s (~2027 for SK hynix/Samsung). Micron-specific: **shipped HBM4 to key customers in June 2025 and moved into high-volume HBM4 production for NVIDIA Vera Rubin in March 2026 (36 GB 12-Hi)**; **HBM4E timeline extends to ~2028** (later than the Koreans' ~2027); uses an **in-house advanced CMOS base die** for HBM4 and **custom base dies with TSMC** for HBM4E — Micron has said HBM4E with **optional base-die customization will carry higher gross margin than standard HBM4E**; its **HBM customer base has expanded to 6 customers**. Value capture is shifting into the logic base die, advanced packaging and substrate (ABF ~100% share), not only DRAM bits (Atlas Peak, 2026-04-03).

- **🆕 2026-09-30 — INSIDE MU'S HBM INTERFACE TEAM: WHY HBM5 PIN SPEED IS A ROUTING/TSV PROBLEM, AND WHY CUSTOM HBM MAY *NARROW* MU'S DESIGN ROLE** (**DAMNANG (Substack)** — "[Expert Call Report] How Is Micron Making HBM Faster?", **2026-09-30**) ⚠️ **INDEPENDENT SUBSTACK AUTHOR, NOT A BROKER — no rating, no price target, no house model.** Expert = a current Micron HBM interface designer (ex-Samsung SSD interface); author's caveats: *"not a verbatim transcript"*, answers *"do not represent the company's official position"*; the 16→32 Gbps figures are *illustrative*, not finalized HBM4E/HBM5 specs. [Source](../Damnang/2026-09-30%20-%20%5BExpert%20Call%20Report%5D%20How%20Is%20Micron%20Making%20HBM%20Faster-.md)
  - _Pin speed is a DRAM problem, not just a base-die problem:_ the DRAM core die cannot run at external pin speed, so the base die deserializes (e.g. 32 Gbps → 4×8 Gbps; ratios of 4:1 / 8:1 / 16:1 are evaluated in advanced development). If DRAM-side speed stays flat while pins double toward HBM5, the internal ratio — and TSV count/routing/area/cost — roughly doubles. Vendors' internal ratios are NOT set by JEDEC and may differ across Samsung/Hynix/MU.
  - _Custom HBM:_ the expert sees [[NVDA]] *"inclined to take on a large share of the design itself"*; if customer IP (controller, external interface, UCIe-style IP) occupies the base die, MU's interface role could shrink to the TSV I/O. Customer-specific TSV placement in 3D-stacked (memory-on-logic) designs would also make the **core die** customer-specific, hurting reuse and raising engineering headcount — MU is packaging non-customer portions as reusable IP to contain that.
  - _Layer count:_ requests for 8-Hi (or fewer) were explained internally by **customer segment / product mix and supply**, not bonding-yield problems; interfaces are still designed for the 12/16-Hi worst case. Consistent with the 8-Hi read-through above — fewer layers ≠ lower capacity demand.
  - _Organisation:_ MU built HBM capability by aggressive external hiring of experienced engineers (vs Samsung's internal task-force pulls) → an "inverted pyramid" now being back-filled with new graduates. The author explicitly says this does NOT establish yields or customer qualification.
  - 🔭 _Variant perception:_ the Street framing is that custom/base-die HBM expands memory makers' value capture; this source argues the opposite risk — customers moving into the base die could cap MU's design scope (and pricing leverage, per the author's NVHBM question) even as stacking advances.

## NAND / storage
- **AI finally reaches NAND (MS, 2025-09-10):** incremental ~$29B AI-inference NAND TAM by 2029; AI NAND ≈34% of global NAND market by 2029. Industry shifts from oversupply (since 2022) to **shortage from 2H26** — ~2% base case, up to ~8% in the bull case as nearline (NL) SSD takes share from NL HDD amid HDD capacity constraints. QLC eSSD is the optimal storage tier for AI (high-capacity, randomized I/O). MS prefers SNDK / Korea names directly; read-through to MU is positive but MU is not MS's NAND top pick. Constructive for MU's ~20% NAND mix into the back half of CY26.

- **LTA/SCA structural-shift thesis — flagged explicitly as a major bull/bear debate item.** Bulls (BNP Paribas' Ackerman via Barron's, 2026-06-29; sell-side broadly, see below) read the 16 take-or-pay contracts (~40% of revenue once fully executed, locked through 2030) as evidence the memory industry itself is "undergoing a transformative shift toward long-term supply agreements which supports demand assurance, through-cycle profitability, and mitigated cyclicality" — i.e. it de-risks the cyclicality that has always capped memory-stock multiples. Bears/skeptics flag the *newness* of the dynamic as the risk, not the reassurance: a SemiAnalysis reader comment (Drew Van Pelt, "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06, p.35 — explicitly a comment, not the SemiAnalysis analyst body) notes the current LTAs are "very different from the past," i.e. a structural break from history that the market/analysts have limited precedent to model — cuts both ways: it could mean the cyclicality is genuinely gone, or it could mean investors are underwriting duration/terms that have never been tested through a real downturn. MU's own Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana concedes the communication gap directly: "We are putting a lot of effort into not only doing these [long-term agreements] but communicating a lot of the details, and it'll take investors some time to understand all the details" (Sadana to Barron's, 2026-06-29) — i.e. even management frames this as a still-developing narrative, not a fully priced-in fact. **Bernstein (Mark Newman) "New Memory LTAs part 2 - Case studies from Microchip" (2026-07-09)** puts the sharpest historical frame on the deposits-as-downside-protection question: Micron backs its memory-LTA obligations with **$18B of cash deposits on its own balance sheet plus $4B in letters of credit**, and — because these upfront guarantees are back-end-weighted, with the **coverage ratio rising toward 75-100% of remaining obligations in the outer years** — they give **"meaningful but not infinite" downside protection**, materially better-structured than the old semiconductor LTAs that broke through prior downturns (Microchip's PSP, Hemlock polysilicon). This is the constructive counter to the "deposits = vendor financing" bear point (@PatrickMoorhead) and the "never tested through a real downturn" skeptic read (Bernstein "New Memory LTAs part 2", 2026-07-09).
- **Bernstein "Memory LTA effectiveness" — the skeptic's quantitative bound on the same LTA debate (Bernstein · Mark Newman, 2026-07-09).** A separate, same-day Bernstein cut (distinct from the constructive "part 2 — Case studies from Microchip" note above; both Newman, 2026-07-09) puts the harder numbers on *how much* protection the deposits actually buy — quantifying the "not infinite" side of the "meaningful but not infinite" conclusion. Bernstein argues LTA effectiveness is **impossible to quantify precisely** (the floor price, market price and the customer's walk-away barrier are all time-dependent, and the barrier *rises* as RPO amortizes). Top-down: the **~$3.33B of deposits secured industry-wide so far is <1% (~0.6%) of the revenue an LTA book would need to protect**; a genuinely "secure" **20% deposit would require ~$1 trillion of customer cash upfront** — "who on earth has that kind of cash today?" On the marquee **Micron–Anthropic deal specifically:** Micron gave a supply guarantee and Anthropic gave back **an equity stake, not cash** — Bernstein calls this **"vendor financing" that does NOT reduce risk for investors** (a sharper, named version of @PatrickMoorhead's generic "deposits = vendor financing" bear). And the **ceiling of LTA coverage is only ~50-67% of the market** (SanDisk's CEO: PC/smartphone "customer-customers" are transactional and won't sign; China customers prefer increasingly-large local suppliers), so a third-to-half of demand stays uncovered. Bear-leaning on the LTA-durability thesis (Bernstein "Memory LTA effectiveness", 2026-07-09). [../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_09_bernstein_on_lta_s.html](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_09_bernstein_on_lta_s.html)
- **Price up, content down — the 2027 HBM-pricing call and the offsetting de-spec, from the buyer's own BOM (SemiAnalysis "Can AMD break the CUDA Moat? AMD Advancing AI 2026", 2026-07-24).** The bull leg first: SemiAnalysis explicitly expects "**a significant increase in HBM pricing in 2027 as memory suppliers move to match the margins they now earn on commodity DRAM**" — i.e. commodity-DRAM margin is now the *anchor* HBM is being repriced toward, the exact inversion this page already tracks (UBS: DDR GM surpassing HBM GM in early C2026; BofA 06-21: chipmakers intend to raise HBM prices aggressively in 2027). It is modelled as strong enough to **compress the accelerator vendors' own margins**: AMD's ASPs must rise but it cannot pass the full memory increase through, because "most of AMD's volume goes to large buyers with real negotiating leverage, and those buyers have more alternatives than they used to," so HBM cost increases pass through "**at a lower incremental margin than their corporate margins, dragging down gross margins on the MI455X package.**" Baseline context: "**HBM, DRAM, and NAND prices alike have increased dramatically since our baseline in mid-2025**" (SemiAnalysis Memory Model / Accelerator and HBM Model). **The bear leg is the same note and is the reason a straight price × prior-content revenue model is wrong.** Tight memory supply is already destroying attach: AMD's original 2025 BOM estimate for the MI455X platform carried "a staggering **138TB in DRAM across LPDDR5X and DDR5 MRDIMM**"; the current estimate has **LPDDR5X entirely removed** plus a **significant DDR5 de-spec to a far lower DDR5 RDIMM content** — specifically the previously-roadmapped **up to 1TB of direct-attached LPDDR per MI455X accelerator on the EAM module has disappeared**, which SemiAnalysis attributes directly to tight memory supply. Its framing is the part to carry: "**much of the DRAM price increases are offset by aggressive de-specs.**" **Why this matters here:** it is the mechanism behind MS/Joe Moore's 07-24 "LTAs and de-speccing could flatten the amplitude of the cycle… but increase duration" line already on this page — now with a named platform and a quantified content cut behind it, sourced from the buyer's BOM rather than from a memory maker. Consensus revenue models that take 2027 HBM/DRAM price up while holding per-accelerator content flat are double-counting; the honest read is **price-led revenue with content as a live offset**. (SemiAnalysis "Can AMD break the CUDA Moat? AMD Advancing AI 2026", 2026-07-24) [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_24_ENC_Can_AMD_break_the_CUDA_Moat_AMD_Advancing_AI_2026_email.html)
- **Historical valuation context (Barron's Streetwise, Jack Hough, June 1 2026 issue):** "A year and a half ago... Micron... was actually the cheapest stock in America relative to earnings. It was about $540 at the start of May [2026]... Now the stock is over $900, and Micron this past week passed a trillion-dollar market value." The same issue's cover story "Rally in Chips" (Barron's/Adam Levine) added: Micron "saw 196% year-over-year sales growth with a 74% gross margin in the most recent quarter... adjusted EPS will grow from $8.29 to over $100 in fiscal 2027... at a recent $924, the stock is trading at just nine times 2027 EPS." Debt reduced 33% over the past three quarters; buying back shares for the first time since 2022. Tech Trader (Adam Levine, same issue) on the supply-lockup dynamic: "Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics... don't have significant new manufacturing coming on-line until the middle of next year [2027]... All of this year's supply is spoken for, and 2027 order books are getting close to full" (Barron's, 2026-06-01).
- **Bull:** This is a durable up-cycle, not a normal one. DB (Melissa Weathers, Buy) raised PT 2026-06-17: "DRAM tightness extends to 2028+; agentic AI drives memory intensity." GS (Schneider) sees "ongoing tightness through CY27; significant upside to Street estimates" (briefing 2026-06-09). The marquee bull is **UBS Arcuri (Buy, PT $1,625, raised from $535)** on a "path to >$100 EPS," LTAs locking ~30% of industry DDR bits and ~$400bn FCF C27-29E (briefings 2026-05-26 / 2026-05-31). Citi (Atif Malik, Buy, PT $840) re-rated to 8x C27 EPS from 5x (2026-05-19); MS reiterates bull case PT $1,050 (2026-06-04). Mechanism: HBM's 3:1 DDR5 die trade-off + node-driven bit decline + multi-year cleanroom lead times keep supply structurally short while LTAs/SCAs convert the equity into an earnings-durability story (JPM memory-China call, 2026-05-28). The UBS 2026 deck adds two structural legs: HBM cannibalizing DDR wafer capacity keeps DDR undersupplied (DDR GM may surpass HBM GM in early C2026), and the longest memory upcycle in 30 years. CPU upside is incremental fuel — NVIDIA Vera standalone CPU ~500k units this year, ~3M next year, could lift total server DRAM demand >15-20% (JPM/Gokul, 2026-05-28).
- **Bear:** Memory is still a commodity and the cycle always turns. The sharpest bear voice on disk is the **ex-VP Procurement (Micron)**, 2026-06-10: the market is pricing peak earnings as a sustainable level — "a highly catastrophic assumption." His view: HBM differentiation is temporary (once a second/third vendor is qualified at each customer it commoditizes like DRAM), Micron's cost structure is worse than Samsung's and roughly at SK Hynix, and "your $900 stock right now will become a $50 stock again" once new fabs (Micron/SK/Samsung) bring disruptive capacity online ~a year out — possibly normalizing "within this calendar year or early next." Two technical bear reads-through support the "differentiation is temporary" thesis: MU is redesigning its HBM4 base die for speed parity and lacks in-house leading-edge logic for custom base dies (Jefferies/Inspectrum + SemiAnalysis) — Samsung's foundry is a structural edge there. He frames the AI buildout as a bull-whip ("beer game") several layers removed from end demand that can't amortize ~$6-700B of infra spend. Second-order: customers are being forced to qualify Chinese suppliers (CXMT) on cheap DRAM Micron won't supply — "once they're in, they're in." UBS's own desk called the Arcuri PT "the most controversial UBS note recently" (briefing 2026-05-31).
- **Buy-side voice — Alex Chaloff (CIO, Bernstein Private Wealth Management), named PM Q&A, Barron's 2026-06-22:** "We are focused on Seagate Technology Holdings and Micron Technology, which have seen over 200% growth this year on the back of significant pickup in spend on memory" — a named, on-record buy-side CIO citing MU (alongside STX) as a core memory-boom holding, corroborating the sell-side consensus from the demand side rather than a bank's own research seat (Barron's/Chaloff, 2026-06-22; see also [STX.md](STX.md) cross-reference).

We don't see more than that"* — best case **70 Micron / 70 Hynix / 80 Samsung** — with the binding constraint named as **cleanroom**, not capital (*"those guys are putting a fab on the ground with one year or… seven months payback… with the [DRAM] price"*), so *"**2028 is still going to be under supply** if the demand keeps growing at the pace as it is right now."* ⚠️ **Unit not stated in the transcript; read as incremental wafer starts per month added per year off the CXMT *"50K of wafer starts"* comparator in the same passage — NOT the same object as this page's 60K-wpm HBM capacity LEVEL for MU or the ~150-200K wpm Korean LEVELS.** **The demand-side rebuttal is his own, immediately:** the **HBM4E→HBM4 de-spec is a *"20% smaller die"* with *"lower stacks"*, so *"the trade ratio starts to SHRINK."* ➤ 🔴 **THIS IS THE DEBATE IN ONE SENTENCE: the undersupply call rests on a fixed wafer ceiling AND on HBM consuming a rising multiple of DRAM wafer per bit. If the ratio shrinks, the same ceiling supports more sellable conventional bits and the shortage is shallower than the wafer math implies.** ⚠️⚠️ **CANONICAL UNCHANGED: `_meta/assumptions.md` `hbm-cycle` stays at **3:1 at HBM3E → ~4:1 at HBM4/4E** (Micron/Sadana 2026-08-10; BMO 08-20; Mizuho 05-27). The shrinking-ratio claim is a DATED VARIANT and a challenge, not a replacement — no canonical number is moved on the strength of an unattributed call.** ✅ **Directionally aligned with the 09-13 SemiAnalysis *"4-hi wins"* block on this page (bandwidth/TCO, tokens-per-wafer) and with the 09-09 expert fragment (buyer cost against ~80% supplier GM) — three mechanisms, one direction, none of them adopted as a bit forecast.** Duration is explicitly NOT underwritten: *"I wouldn't be willing to put in my model that the under supply is going to last until 2029."*

## Risks
- ASP volatility / cyclicality — 10-K flags "significant volatility in average selling prices" and cash-flow/operating-result volatility that can pressure the credit rating (FY25 10-K).
- Commodity normalization — capacity from Micron/SK/Samsung new fabs landing ~CY27-28 could break the price structure (ex-VP, 2026-06-10).
- Cost-structure disadvantage vs Samsung (geographically dispersed footprint); roughly at SK Hynix (ex-VP, 2026-06-10).
- HBM4 base-die execution — MU redesigning the base die for speed parity and dependent on TSMC/IP partners for advanced logic; Samsung's in-house foundry is an edge (Jefferies/Inspectrum 2025-12-17; SemiAnalysis 2025-08-12).
- **HBM4 pin-speed / qualification risk — sharper version of the above.** SemiAnalysis is explicitly "skeptical of execution" on MU's HBM4 given samples showing much lower pin speeds than Samsung/SK Hynix, and forecasts ~0% MU share of Rubin HBM supply in the first 12 months (SemiAnalysis "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06, p.29) — a more bearish read than the "redesigning for parity" framing elsewhere on this page; watch for qualification updates that resolve this either way. Related capacity risk: the A3 (Idaho) and newly acquired P5 Tongluo fabs are not expected to contribute meaningful output until mid/2H-2027 at the earliest (SemiAnalysis "Memory Mania," 2026-02-06, p.23,30), so near-term HBM capacity upside is capped regardless of demand.
- Geopolitics/regulation — export restrictions, tariffs, trade measures; China DRAM substitution via CXMT gaining low-end LPDDR share (10-K; JPM 2026-05-28).
- **🆕🔴🔴🔴 CXMT PASSES MICRON ON WAFER CAPACITY IN 2028 — THE FIRST NAMED-HOUSE MODEL TO PUT A DATE AND A RANK ON THE CHINA RISK, AND IT COMES FROM AN *INITIATION ON CXMT ITSELF* RATHER THAN FROM A MICRON NOTE (Bernstein · Mark Li / Edward Hou / Yipin Cai, "China Next Winners: CXMT — Redrawing the Memory Map", 2026-09-21; CXMT 688825.CH **Outperform, PT CNY 70.00**).** Bernstein models CXMT wafer capacity **300k wpm now → 380k 4Q27 → 530k 4Q28 (+~75%)**, funded by capex of **CNY 81 / 142 / 236bn (US$12 / 21 / 35bn) in 2026/27/28** — *"We project CXMT's wafer capacity share may **surpass Micron in 2028**, reaching nearly **20% globally**."* Discounted for lower bit density, **bit share ~9% (2026) → 12% (2028)**, conventional-DRAM-only **~10% → 14%**, revenue share **10% → 13%**, lifting China's DRAM self-sufficiency **42% → 58%**. The uncomfortable part is not the capacity, it is the margin: **CXMT's 2Q26 DRAM gross margin was 88%, *"as good as 87-89% from Samsung, SK hynix & Micron"***, and Bernstein's EBITDA-margin work says CXMT was *"already competitive on cash cost"* **before** the price surge — *"similar EBITDA margin implies similar cash cost, and hence that CXMT's ability to weather future downturns is likely similar to the global incumbents too."* On the technology gate the read is two-sided: G4 is **1z-1a nm, c. 3-4 years behind**, and HBM is genuinely hard (export control caps imported tooling at **>3000 TSVs/die** against SK hynix's **>5600 in HBM3 and >20000 in HBM4**; base dies are moving to advanced logic nodes China cannot make) — *but* **"DUV is sufficient to sustain CXMT for another 3-5 years"**, explicitly because *"Micron does not adopt EUV until 1gamma nm."* **MU's own EUV-lateness, logged elsewhere on this page as a relative-laggard flag, is the evidence Bernstein uses to argue China does not need EUV yet.** ⚠️⚠️ **DO NOT MERGE WITH THE UBS MARK IN THE SAME WEEK — they are ~18 months apart on the same variable: UBS has CXMT DRAM bit supply share **~7% C2025 → ~9% C2027** and calls the concern *"a bit overstated"*; Bernstein has ~9% already in 2026. Both stand; neither adopted.** ⚠️ **Bernstein's own two flagged risks are worth carrying because they cut its case: minority interests took **63% of consolidated profit in 2H25** (25-29% in 1H26) and are *"a major risk to our EPS projection"*, and **2.2% of shares unlock 27-Jan-2027 with a further 33% on 27-Jul-2027**. [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/BERN_260453.html)
- **China DRAM capacity build-out accelerating beyond CXMT — new long-dated supply overhang.** China's government is working with state-run **Huawei + state-invested SwaySure** to build a **Shenzhen DRAM complex of 140,000 wpm (12-inch), 28nm DRAM**, with ex-TSMC fab director **Steve Liu hired as CEO** and the ex-president of **Elpida** (which Micron acquired) as head strategist; supply-chain reports describe SwaySure as a Huawei "shadow fab" (alongside PXW/PXX) (@dnystedt, 2026-07-15). Sizing the aggregate: @zephyr_z9's 2030-vs-2026 capacity work (via @EugeneNg, 2026-07-15) has **total global DRAM capacity >2x (+128%) by 2030**, the big-3 (Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron) **~2x (+92%)**, **CXMT ~3x (+171%)** and **all of China ~4x (+303%)** with CXMT/YMTC/SwaySure/JHICC — i.e. China grows off a low base far faster than the incumbents, feeding the bear's eventual-oversupply timing debate (low-end/28nm today, not a near-term server/HBM threat). Fresh Korean capacity adds are also landing (Samsung new Giheung DRAM fab ~100k wpm; SK Hynix accelerating its Yongin "Y1" fab, initial ~20k wpm equipment orders — @jukan05, 2026-07-14) — years out, but incremental supply nonetheless.
- **De-spec / content destruction — the under-modelled offset to the price melt-up (SemiAnalysis, 2026-07-24 and 2026-07-21).** Distinct from demand elasticity in consumer: the accelerator platforms themselves are cutting DRAM attach *because* memory is scarce and expensive. On AMD's MI455X, the **up-to-1TB per-accelerator direct-attached LPDDR tier has been removed outright** and DDR5 de-spec'd to a far lower RDIMM content vs an original 2025 BOM of **138TB of DRAM per platform across LPDDR5X + DDR5 MRDIMM** ("much of the DRAM price increases are offset by aggressive de-specs" — SemiAnalysis "Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?", 2026-07-24). The same pattern in the custom parts is a direct HBM-content cut: **Meta's custom MI450/MI455 halves the compute silicon and cuts HBM from 12 stacks to 6 per package, and downgrades the HBM4 from 12-Hi to 8-Hi** — at one of AMD's two largest GPU customers, on a program SemiAnalysis argues "is going to nuke AMD's volume at Meta because TBD will vastly prefer Rubin," so the HBM-content read is **doubly negative: fewer stacks per package on a program that may itself shrink** (SemiAnalysis "Meta's Infrastructure Team Needs A Culture Reset", 2026-07-21; same conclusion restated 2026-07-24). The risk to Micron is not the DRAM price deck — it is **bits per accelerator**, which the Street generally holds flat or growing. [Source](../relat%C3%B3rios%20bons/2026_07_21_ENC_Metas_Infrastructure_Team_Needs_A_Culture_Reset_email.html)
  - **Management's direct answer — and it concedes the fact while contesting the cause (Micron IR call · Satish, 2026-07-27).** Asked whether new systems could require less memory by 2028, Satish conceded the observable: "**customers are actually reducing the rate of content growth for memory versus their prior plans, because there is just not enough supply available**" — server units are growing faster than per-server memory, "so the ratio decreases, so the content is expected to grow at a slower rate compared to what customers were previously saying **because of the supply constraint**." But he frames it as a **supply artifact, not a real optimization**: "it's… more a supply related issue **as opposed to an optimization that truly reduces the amount of memory you need per unit of hardware**." On genuine efficiency work (sparse attention, compression, mixture-of-experts) his answer is Jevons — cheaper tokens drive more users *and* longer context/more aggressive agentic workflows, "a net positive in terms of overall demand" — supported by **two Micron white papers published in the last few months (one the prior week)** showing that more LPDDR content raises token throughput and that more HBM4 content or bandwidth does the same. **Why this matters for the bear case:** SemiAnalysis's de-spec evidence and management's account are *not contradictory* — both say bits per unit are being cut today. They differ only on whether the cut **reverses when supply arrives** (management) or **persists as a re-architected BOM** (SemiAnalysis). That is now the single testable question on the content axis, and neither side has settled it. (Micron IR call · Satish, 2026-07-27)
- **Antitrust / price-fixing litigation** — the 06-30 N.D. Cal. class action (17 plaintiffs) is a new legal-risk item on the "big three colluding to keep DRAM scarce" narrative (media report via @dnystedt, 2026-06-30).
- HBM share/competition — SK Hynix leadership (NVIDIA multiyear tech partnership), Samsung HBM4 qualifying and ~20% share rising (Jefferies/Inspectrum 2025-12-17); customers dual-source by design.
- Demand elasticity in price-sensitive PC/smartphone/consumer segments at elevated ASPs (Mehrotra, 2025-12-17).

_**Síntese do quarter — opened 2026-10-01 (F1Q27 window; no post-print source yet):** the print settled the near-term numbers (revenue, EPS, FQ1 revenue guide all above every bogey on the page) and moved the debate to three places. ① **Margin path:** FQ1 ~86.25% is the declared FY27 floor — BofA's "mid-80s" bogey is met; the ~91% UBS peak now has to come from FQ2 onward with "more moderate" price increases. ② **Content:** management's "modestly lower rate of content growth" is the first company-side admission behind the de-spec debate — the window's open question (bits per accelerator) is now partly answered by management, against the bulls. ③ **Supply timing:** a construction-led FY27 capex raise (>~$50bn implied) targets cleanroom for late-CY28+, so the late-2028 supply debate (DAMNANG 09-15, DB 09-16) is now the live bear test. Q&A (pending) is where the buyback size, HBM share and FY27 GM range would show up._

(3) MEMORY AT ~50% OF SYSTEM VALUE (from ~10% three decades ago), with the KV-cache mechanism spelled out — "poor KV cache handling forces GPUs to RECOMPUTE PRIOR WORK rather than advance new work, which INFLATES UTILIZATION METRICS WITHOUT PRODUCING REAL OUTPUT" — and the stated tiering: HBM for the hot path, SOCAMM2 main memory for KV overflow, disaggregated DDR5 pools for the long tail. (4) A NEW DEMAND LEG: hyperscalers now "addressing UNDERINVESTMENT ON THE CPU SIDE as workloads shift from human-driven to agent-driven execution," with agentic adoption at a "PRE-SEASON WARM-UP" stage — corroborating the agentic-CPU thesis from [[AMD]]/[[INTC]]/[[ARM]] from the memory side.**

**Source: Deutsche Bank · Melissa Weathers / Joe Schwab / DJ Sebastian — *"Global Memory: Chipping away at industry supply imbalance"* (TMT Industry Update · Semiconductors, 14pp, **2026-09-16**, distributed 09-17).** ⚠️ **THIS IS A SECOND, SEPARATE DB DOCUMENT from the 09-16 MU preview in (4) above** (*"Reiterate Buy into earnings as fundamentals stay stronger for longer"*, 10pp) — **same house, same three authors, same date, different note.** It carries **MU at Buy, px $927.60**, and publishes **NO price target**, so the **$1,550 PT in (1) is untouched and NOTHING ON THIS PAGE IS SUPERSEDED.**

🔴🔴🔴 **THE FINDING, AND IT IS THE ANSWER TO (5): ON THE UNIT DB'S MODEL IS ACTUALLY BUILT IN, THE DEMAND-OVER-SUPPLY WEDGE IS ~1 POINT — AND IT RUNS IN SUPPLY'S FAVOUR.** Both sides are published, both over **2025-30**, both in k WSPM: **required DRAM wafer starts 1,921k (2025) → 3,634k (2030) = +14% CAGR**, against **estimated DRAM WSPM capacity 1,921k (2025) → 3,796k (2030) = +15% CAGR** — **both growth figures are DB's own, printed in its "2025-30 Growth" column.** ➤ **The +21% bit-demand CAGR is already INSIDE the +14% required-wafer line.** DB converts bits to wafers explicitly: bit/wafer density gains **−8% / −8% / −6% / −6% / −6% y/y**, yield gains **−5%/yr** (standard DRAM) and **−5% then −8%/yr** (HBM), offset by an HBM trade-ratio uplift of **+5% / +8% / +3% / +3% / +3%**. **So "21% vs 15%" is not a six-point shortage — differencing them double-counts the density and yield gains, exactly as (5) warned. DB's own shortage is the gap between +14% required and +15% available, and it is a TIMING phenomenon (capacity arrives two-to-three years late), not a structural deficit.**

Specifically: Samsung said 60-70% OF ITS MEMORY SALES WILL BE UNDER LTA, but with ASYMMETRIC terms — a price-cut FLOOR of sub-5% down q/q against price INCREASES broadly open at 10-20%+. High LTA coverage is therefore bullish for realised ASP stability rather than a cap on it, which is the opposite of how rising contract coverage is usually read at this point in a cycle.** **Spot: sentiment positive into August on three drivers — (1) chip order increases for inventory restocking; (2) many Tier-2 OEMs resuming smartphone/PC launches for Sept/4Q DESPITE high memory cost; (3) China domestic smartphone shipments bottoming out — only 17MN UNITS IN JUNE vs a normal 25-30mn, with lean channel inventories. ⚠️ Note the DRAM/NAND divergence in the confirmed July contract prints: TrendForce July DRAM contract price UP LOW-TEENS % M/M = 30-50% Q/Q, but FLAT FOR NAND.** **On China supply, the reason it is not showing up in spot: "minimal impact from China local chipmakers' capacity expansion — China-branded memory NOT COMMONLY TRADED IN THE SPOT MARKET; even Korea/US/Japan chips not much available for white-box OEMs."** Adjacent confirmation that the AI-server pull is broad: **SEMCO and LG Innotek both guided bullishly on AI MLCC and FC-BGA, with 2Q OP more than doubling y/y, stronger LTA orders, LARGE PREPAYMENTS funding new fab construction, and contract price increases through 2H and 2027 — and all three top MLCC makers (SEMCO, Murata, Taiyo Yuden) have raised prices.** |
